newsitem.title: GERMANY: MOTOR RACING-BERGER POLE DELIVERS LONG-AWAITED JOY FOR BENETTON.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-BERGER POLE DELIVERS LONG-AWAITED JOY FOR BENETTON.

text.p: Austrian Gerhard Berger returned to competitive action with a vengeance on Saturday when he delivered the Benetton team's long-awaited first pole position since the departure in 1995 of their German world champion Michael Schumacher.

Berger, 37, secured the prime grid position for Sunday's German Grand Prix in his Renault-powered car, eclipsing his nearest rival Giancarlo Fisichella of Italy in a Peugeot-powered Jordan by 0.023 seconds after dominating the qualifying session.

The gap between him and Fisichella, whose front-row position is the best of his career, may not have appeared decisive, but was sufficient to prove Berger had recovered from his difficulties of recent months.

Berger missed the last three races following sinus surgery, but stunned the huge crowd at the high-speed Hockenheim track in the forests south of Heidelberg by clocking the fastest time early in the session and then trimming it in the final 15 minutes.

Two days after announcing he would not drive for Benetton next season, Berger mounted a perfect demonstration of talent and experience and showed his strength of character as his father had died in an aircraft crash during his absence from the track.

Jokingly, Berger agreed that it would suit him to sign a contract that gave him one race on and three off. "It is a boost to my confidence and also for the team," he said. "We have had a very difficult time this year. But the race will be very different and I will be very glad to finish on the podium."
Fisichella was in turn just 0.1 of a second ahead of Finland's Mika Hakkinen in a McLaren, powered by Mercedes-Benz, who was third. The top nine were separated by only a second.
Double world champion and current series leader Michael Schumacher of Germany was fourth fastest in a Ferrari just ahead of another German Heinz-Harald Frentzen in a Williams Renault who was fifth.
Schumacher's 22-year-old younger brother Ralf, the third German driver, in the second Jordan, was seventh behind Frenchman Jean Alesi in the second Benetton. Alesi was sixth.
Villeneuve, in the other Williams, was unable to improve on ninth place behind Briton David Coulthard in the second McLaren. Briton Eddie Ivine in the second Ferrari was 10th.
World champion Damon Hill of Britain was a creditable 13th in his Yamaha-powered Arrows car on a circuit where outright speed and engine strength matters more than elsewhere.
Berger's pole position was his first since the Belgian Grand Prix at Spa-Francorchamaps in 1995 -- 32 races ago.
It was also the 12th pole of his career on the eve of his 203rd Grand Prix giving him a chance to make up for last year's race when his engine failed while he was leading with only one lap remaining.

Fisichella said he was delighted with his grid position and denied that he had any problems with his team mate Ralf Schumacher, with whom he had a row earlier this year after the Argentine Grand Prix where they collided. "We are friends now and we are working together with no problems," he said.

Hakkinen said he may have gone quicker but for time he lost early in the weekend with engine problems and when Berger spun in front of him in the closing stages of the session. "I feel very confident," he said.
Asked if he could guess why the two Williams drivers struggled in fifth and ninth positions, he said: "The drivers, I guess."
The Williams team were using the same specification Renault V10s as the Benetton team, but had failed to make as much use of them.
